summary: Bass River Light, 1855, at the mouth of the Bass River: dark 1880, relit 1881, out 1914, privately relit 1989; now the Lighthouse Inn's tower.

structures.type: lantern on the roof of a wood keeper's house

access.note: The light is part of the Lighthouse Inn. Grounds are open to the public; the tower is not a public climb. Ask the inn before visiting.

stay.note: The Lighthouse Inn takes overnight guests

facts.agency: The Lighthouse Inn (privately owned and maintained since 1989)

events.note: Construction began 1 May 1854; house and tower completed winter 1855
Fifth-order Fresnel, fixed white (New England Lighthouses, booklet); archive says fourth order
Discontinued 1 August 1880 after Stage Harbor light built; sold at auction 1 September 1880
Reinstated and lit 1 July 1881; Samuel Peak appointed keeper
Extinguished 15 June 1914 after Cape Cod Canal opened; last fifth-order lens removed
Automatic light established on the Bass River west jetty
Relit 7 August 1989 by private owners, for the Lighthouse Service's 200th anniversary

corrections.why: The booklet quotes the Light List entry: 12 miles, 10.43 nautical miles. No source read gives 7 nm.
The booklet and New England Lighthouses both say fifth order; the archive says fourth. Not applied; check the Light List and a primary source.

corrections.proposed: add 1880 deactivated (1 August) and 1881 relit (1 July)
corrections.why: The light was discontinued in 1880 and relit in 1881, which the archive roster's continuous 1881-1906 keeper line also reflects.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The light was relit on 7 August 1989 by private owners and is recognized by the Coast Guard, so it is lit now; the 1914 date is the last federal extinguishing.
The 1880 shut-down and 1881 relight, which some sources omit, explain why the roster has a keeper from 1881 after a 1869-1880 keeper.
New England Lighthouses and the booklet's 1914 entry say a fifth-order Fresnel lens; the U.S. Lighthouse Society place record says fourth order, installed 1855. Not resolved; the story states both.
The booklet gives 30 April 1855 (chronology) and 1 May 1855 (introduction); New England Lighthouses gives 30 April 1855. The story gives both.

The booklet gives February 1854 and the seller George Richardson with his wife Phebe; New England Lighthouses gives March 1854 and George W. Richardson. The story gives the booklet's date and notes the other.
The booklet gives Wixon $500 a year from payroll records; New England Lighthouses gives $350, the same as Chase. The story states both.

The booklet gives 25 cents per month in its introduction and 25 cents annually in its 1841-era passage (other sources say monthly); New England Lighthouses gives monthly. The story states the booklet's two versions.

The booklet calls William Garfield a cousin of President James Garfield; New England Lighthouses says distant relative. The booklet says the President invited the captain and his two daughters to the White House; New England Lighthouses says they were invited to dinner. Both attributed in the story.

notes_for_editor: (1) Discontinuance: the booklet, Dennis Historical Society and New England Lighthouses give 1880 shut-down and 1881 relight; the record has only 1914. The archive roster's Peak line (1881-1906) fits the relight. (2) First lit: 30 April 1855 (booklet chronology; New England Lighthouses) vs 1 May 1855 (booklet front page; inn). (3) Land: booklet says February 1854 from George Richardson and his wife Phebe for $75; New England Lighthouses says March 1854 from George W. Richardson. (4) Wixon's pay: booklet $500; New England Lighthouses says $350 like Chase. (5) Auction after 1914: booklet cover says 1915, booklet text says 1917; the inn's page says Brown bought the land and sold it to Noyes a few years later. (6) The Garfield anecdote comes from the booklet, which quotes Dan Pierce, The Register (27 May 2010), and New England Lighthouses gives the same dinner date. No government record of the letters or the dinner is cited by either source; the story says so. (7) Lens order: the archive says fourth order; the booklet and New England Lighthouses say fifth. Disputed, not applied. (8) Chronicling America search: 'Bass River light' and 'Peak' in Massachusetts papers, 1881-1914, returned no hits. No storm, wreck or rescue tied to the station was found, so the story has no storms chapter. (9) The Light List range (10.43 nm) is from the booklet's header, not checked against the current Light List. (10) The Lighthouse Board annual reports in the local corpus (1891-1901) list Bass River only in index and survey lists; not used. The 1880 and 1881 reports are not in the corpus. (11) Wikipedia was consulted for orientation only and is not cited. The inn's own history is a promotional source and is used only for ownership dates it shares with the booklet. (12) Current owners are named only as the inn's public management (third generation of the Stone family); no private family details are included. | CHECK 2026-10-27: the record's 1880/1881 and 1914 dates are confirmed by the booklet, New England Lighthouses and the Dennis Historical Society. The booklet's Garfield story is second-hand from Dan Pierce, The Register (27 May 2010); the story attributes it to the booklet and says the booklet's only citation is that article. The Ryder 1972 memoir appears only as the booklet quotes it; one quotation. The 1914 Cape Cod Canal reason is paraphrased from the booklet, not quoted. Roster lines were checked against archives.uslhs.org/places/bass-river and match.
